newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Keppel bank deal fails to excite analysts.
newsitem.headline: Keppel bank deal fails to excite analysts.

text.p: Shiprepair conglomerate Keppel Corp's purchase of an ailing Philippine bank was a good strategic diversification but was unlikely to add to earnings, analysts said on Friday.

"Strategically, it is good to see Keppel diversifying and trying to break into the Philippines banking sector. But, the deal doesn't look outright positive for Keppel," an analyst with a European institution told Reuters.

Keppel Corp signed a rescue package for Monte de Piedad and Savings Bank, previously majority-owned by the Catholic Church before the Archdiocese of Manila sold it to Vincent Tan in 1995. Under the agreement, signed on Thursday and approved by the Philippines central bank, Keppel will inject one billion pesos (US$37.9 million) to rehabilitate the bank.
It had also promised to provide additional resources to stabilise the bank and quickly regain the public trust and confidence.

Keppel, which is increasingly diversifying away from the shipyard business into property, banking and telecommunications, outbid Indonesia's Lippo Bank in the tussle for control of the Philippines second oldest bank.
Lippo also offered to pump in one billion pesos. But Tan, the majority shareholder exercised his rights of refusal and opted for Keppel.

Teo Soon Hoe, Keppel's group finance director, said the group would work to re-open the bank on May 8. Monte de Piedad was closed temporarily for two weeks after a run on its deposits following rumours that it had 1.8 billion pesos worth of uncollected debt.
Teo said Keppel hoped to add at least six more branches within the first year after the re-opening.
Most analysts said the deal was unlikely to generate any earnings contribution for the group in the near term.
They said the bank's doubtful debt clouded the investment and, based on existing financial information, was a major concern.
"We don't know the exposure. The one billion pesos injection could just be the tip of an iceberg," said an analyst with another European institution.
"The doubtful debt is speculated to be over a billion pesos and Keppel is likely to have to inject more capital to rehabilitate it," she said.
Financing of the takeover was also a worry, analysts said.

"While one billion pesos may not seem like a huge sum for Keppel Corp, it certainly is at company level," said an analyst with a local house. As of end 1996, the company's net debt was at Singapore $760 million.
They said Keppel had some warrants expiring in June which could see some S$420 million in funds coming in.

But analysts said Keppel would need to pay a premium differential of S$800 million to S$1 billion in cash to re-develop its 3.5 million sq ft Singapore yard into a proposed residential and commercial property site.
"That's a lot of upfront money before you see any gains," said one analyst.
